name: Boa-Yewu / leɓóale

catalog_quote: Boa-Yewu is a tone language with two underlying tones, High (H) and Low (L). A tone is associated with a tone-bearing unit. A High and a Low tone can be combined on one tone bearing unit. Tone in Boa-Yewu has a distinctive function, both in the lexicon and in the grammar. The number of tonal minimal pairs in the lexicon is limited. Tone plays a higher functional load in the grammar, examples are given in Sections 2.6 and 2.7. Verb roots have either a High or a Low tone. ... In the CVCV-nouns in my data, only contrasts between L and H are attested. ... LowHigh and HighLow tones are probably composite contours, a sequence of two level tones. Surface contour tones can be seen as the result of association of two tones to one tone bearing unit, after consonant or vowel loss or after vowel coalescence in morphosyntactic environments. In Boa-Yewu, LH and HL are contrastive in the noun system (mostly in CV-nouns) [de Wit 2020: 421-422]. || 2.1.4. Tons / 2.1.4.1. Inventaire / Il existe deux tons simples bas (`) et haut (´) ainsi que deux complexes montant (ˇ) et descendant (ˆ). Le ton bas n'est pas représenté par économie. ... 2.1.4.2. Valeur des tons / Les tons ont une double valeur: lexicale et grammaticale. [Motingea 2005: 30]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.translation: Motingea 2005: 'There are two simple tones, low and high, as well as two complex ones, rising and falling. ... The tones have a double value: lexical and grammatical.'

Sec. 2.4 syllable structure V/CV/…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Boa (both the Yewu dialect of Bambesa and the leɓóale of Buta) is described as a two-tone (H/L) Bantu language with lexical and grammatical tone and surface contour tones from two tones on one TBU; neither modern description, nor the older colonial materials, says anything about word stress or accent placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Motingea notes vowel length arising from coalescence/contact, i.e. a mora distinction, and H-tone 'proéminence' in HL/LH contraction, which is tonal neutralisation, not stress.)
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statements concern the word (lexical roots, CVCV nouns) and verbal inflection; no phrase-level prominence or intonation discussed. de Wit describes the Yewu dialect (Bambesa territory; Guthrie C402), Motingea 2005 the leɓóale of Buta (C44) and the lebaate (Benza/Bati) variety.
new_statements.identity_note: de Wit 2020 describes Boa-Yewu, the Bambesa-territory dialect (Ethnologue 'Bwa' [bww]; Maho C402), which Glottolog subsumes under bwaa1238; Motingea 2005 describes leɓóale/libóali of Buta (C44, the other main Boa dialect) and, in ch. 3, lebaate (Benza/Bati, also filed under bwaa1238 by Glottolog via Koloma 1993 'baati'). Motingea & Kadite 2022 concerns letakpú, a near-extinct secret register of the Bokpendú Boa, not the everyday language. Halkin 1910 / de Calonne 1909 'Ababua, libwâlè/libati' = the same two dialect groups. Not to be confused with Lebéo/Ngelima (Gérard 1924; C45, ngel1238) or Pagibete (C401, pagi1244).

new_statements.quote: Dans son fonctionnement le leɓóale utilise trente-deux phonèmes dont sept phonèmes vocaliques oraux /i, e, ɛ , a, ɔ, o, u /, dix-neuf phonèmes consonantiques /m, n, ɲ, ŋ, b, p , d, t, ɓ,ɗ, g, k, gb, kp, v, s, z, f, l/, deux phonèmes semi-vocaliques / y et w/ et auxquels s'ajoutent quatre tonèmes : deux ponctuels (haut et bas) et deux modulés (montant et descendant). Du point de vue paradigmatique, la syllabe présente une structure ouverte allant d'une simple voyelle à une séquence de plusieurs phonèmes : (N) (C) (S) V-.
new_statements.translation: In its functioning, leɓóale uses thirty-two phonemes: seven oral vowel phonemes /i, e, ɛ, a, ɔ, o, u/, nineteen consonant phonemes /m, n, ɲ, ŋ, b, p, d, t, ɓ, ɗ, g, k, gb, kp, v, s, z, f, l/, two semi-vowel phonemes /y and w/, to which are added four tonemes: two level (high and low) and two contour (rising and falling). From the paradigmatic point of view, the syllable has an open structure ranging from a single vowel to a sequence of several phonemes: (N)(C)(S)V-.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record and de Wit 2020 (tone language, no stress statement). It counts four tonemes where de Wit posits two underlying tones (H, L) with H+L combinable on one TBU; that is a difference of analysis (surface contours vs underlying tones), not a different prosodic type. Describes the leyeu (Yewu) variety of Buta territory, i.e. the same variety as de Wit's 'Boa-Yewu'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The article is a verb-morphology study; its one-paragraph phonological summary lists four tonemes (H, L, rising, falling) alongside the segmental inventory and open (N)(C)(S)V syllables. The words accent, stress, prominence or their French equivalents do not occur anywhere in the 19-page text (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text layer), so the work makes no statement on word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Tekabileba 2026 explicitly studies 'le leyeu, variante du leɓóale parlée dans le territoire de Buta' (p. 350), i.e. the Yewu dialect (Glottolog yewu1238 under bwaa1238), the same variety de Wit 2020 calls Boa-Yewu; it also names leɓááti, legolo and lebɛ́ngɛ as other Boa varieties of Aketi and Bondo territories. Boone & Olson 2004 (per Glottolog language code) covers Bwa-Buta, Benge and Pagibete [pae] as a survey of the whole Bwa bloc.

new_statements.quote: p. 29: "2.4.1 Phonetic. The languages under study all have about the same phonological inventory: all have seven vowels, for example, and all have two implosive stops (bilabial and alveolar) and voiced and voiceless double stops." p. 31 (Table 4a): "stone, plantain lebogo leboko (The tones of 'stone' and 'plantain' contrast)". p. 32: "Note that not only do the vowels coalesce, leaving a single-length vowel, but so do the high and low tones, leaving a falling tone."

All three quoted passages found verbatim with extracted text per page: PDF p. 29 ends with '2.4 Linguistic Findings / 2.4.1 Phonetic / The languages under study all have about the same phonological inventory: all have seven vowels, for example, and all hav…
new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the existing statement (de Wit 2020: two-tone H/L language, tone lexically and grammatically distinctive; no stress statement). Adds nothing on stress; the passing remarks (lexical tone contrast, H+L -> falling) match de Wit's H/L analysis. The report covers the whole 'Bwa bloc' (Pagibete, Boenge-Bati, Bwa = leBoa-le of Buta/Bambesa/Banalia, Kango, Ngoeloema); the tone remarks are stated for the Bwa Bloc dialects generally, with the Table 4a forms from Boenge-Bati vs Pagibete/Bwa-east.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sociolinguistic/dialect survey; its only phonology section (2.4.1) is segmental (7 vowels, implosives, labial-velars, [k]-loss, voicing neutralisation in Boenge-Bati). Tone appears only in passing: a lexical tonal minimal pair (lebogo 'stone' vs 'plantain') and H+L coalescing to a falling tone after [k]-loss. Nothing anywhere in the 91 pages on word stress, accent or prominence (full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/pitch returned no linguistic hits).
new_statements.identity_note: Boone & Olson 2004 treats the 'Bwa bloc' as a whole (Pagibete, Boenge-Bati, Bwa proper = leBoa-le spoken around Buta, Bambesa and Banalia, plus Kango and Ngoeloema); statements in sec. 2.4.1 are comparative across these varieties rather than a description of Boa-Yewu alone.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Sec. 2.4 Tonologie (par. 11): notation too unreliable to treat tone; provisionally two registers (bas, haut), no complex tone observed; melodic H in past narrative as in most 'Bóa bloc' languages. Describes a near-extinct secret/warrior register of the Bokpendú Boa, not the main language; cites Motingea 2019b ms. 'Notes sur le système tonologique du ɓóa-yéwú'.

Leboale sec. 2.1.4 Tons (pp. 30-35): 'Il existe deux tons simples bas et haut ainsi que deux complexes montant et descendant'; tones have lexical and grammatical value; rules: contraste tonal, harmonie tonale, neutralisation, abaissement. 2.1.5 Syllabes (p. 35): open syllables V, (N)CV, (N)CSV, N; vowel section (p. 12) notes long vowels from contact/coalescence = mora distinction.
